frameworks.name: Culture as Rules and Reinforcement
frameworks.definition: A system of spoken and unspoken conditional rules (if-then statements) that govern what behaviors are rewarded, punished, or ignored within an organization.

frameworks.name: Values as Chunked Rules
frameworks.definition: Condensing hundreds of behavioral rules into 3-5 value statements; each value, when unpacked, maps to a coherent set of conditionals that reinforce aligned behavior.

frameworks.name: Context-Specific Rule Definition
frameworks.definition: Identifying and codifying all behavioral rules within specific interaction contexts (meetings, client calls, decision-making) before generalizing to org-wide values.

claims.text: Culture is fundamentally a system of rules, spoken and unspoken, that govern reinforcement in an organization. These rules take the form of conditional statements: if you do this, you will be rewarded; if you do this, nothing happens; if you do this, you will be punished.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Entrepreneurs struggle to improve culture because they cannot define it. Attempting to fix something without a clear definition makes improvement nearly impossible—the first step is establishing an operational definition of what culture means in your specific organization.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Without definitional clarity, improvement efforts are directionless and unmeasurable.

claims.text: Culture cannot be transposed between organizations through osmosis (casual exposure and observation alone). Understanding culture requires observing 100+ behavioral rules and their reinforcement conditions over an extended period; codification is required to transfer culture deliberately between locations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when hiring new team members into a new environment
claims.mechanism: Rules must be explicit because the number of implicit rules exceeds what new members can absorb through observation alone; codification transforms implicit culture into transferable systems.

numbers.axis: number of behavioral rules in an organization

claims.text: Values are best created by first identifying all behavioral rules you want to reinforce, then chunking them into 3-5 high-level value statements. Each value, when unpacked, maps back to a coherent set of conditional rules (if-then behaviors) that define what the value means in practice.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Chunking rules into values creates a memorable, teachable shorthand; unpacking values back to rules enables consistent enforcement and new-member onboarding.

numbers.axis: number of value statements for representing behavioral rules

bounded_by: The 'fast and dirty' approach (vague value descriptions without rule unpacking) trades completeness for speed but creates ambiguity in enforcement.

claims.text: To codify culture systematically, think about the conditions in which people interact within your organization (meetings, pitches, client calls, decision-making sessions). For each context, list all the rules of engagement and conditional reinforcements. These context-specific rule sets aggregate into your org-wide values.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when first codifying culture in an organization
claims.mechanism: Context-specific rules are easier to identify and teach because people can picture the situation; aggregating across contexts creates a comprehensive rule set that drives values.

claims.text: When transposing culture to a new location (e.g., opening a second office), the leader at that location must adhere to the same rules and reinforcement patterns as the original. Culture can only be transferred if both the written rules and the leader's visible behavior model those rules consistently.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: when new leaders inherit codified culture
claims.mechanism: Leaders are the primary reinforcement agents in an organization; if leaders violate the stated rules, the culture collapses because the conditional (rule → reward) is broken.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the original culture champion moves with the leader to the new location to anchor culture initially.

claims.text: At Alex Hormozi's Acquisition.com, a meeting rule is: if you are not talking in a meeting, you must be muted (listening). If you talk when you should be muted (not contributing to the full group), that violates the rule and is grounds for termination, because it signals you are not paying attention to the group context.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The rule enforces presence and attention; violation signals disrespect and disengagement, indicating the person should not be in the role.
bounded_by: This is a specific instantiation of a broader culture rule at Acquisition.com; it may not apply to other organizations with different communication norms.

claims.text: To verify that culture has been successfully transferred to a new location, ensure that the new leader adheres to the codified rules and reinforcement patterns without constant oversight. If culture needs the original culture champion present to sustain itself, it has not been transferred—it is still dependent on that individual.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Culture transfer is complete when the rules are so deeply embedded in leadership behavior and organizational structure that reinforcement happens automatically, not through the originating champion's presence.

examples.text: At Acquisition.com, if you are not contributing to a group meeting, you must be muted to signal attention and respect. If you talk when you are supposed to be listening, that violates the organizational rule and is grounds for immediate termination, because it indicates you are not paying attention to the group—a sign you should not be in the role.

practices.text: Identify the conditions in which your team interacts (meetings, pitches, client calls, one-on-ones) and list all the behavioral rules and reinforcement patterns that should apply in each context.

Codify all behavioral rules you want to reinforce, then chunk them into 3-5 high-level values; ensure each value, when unpacked, maps back to a specific set of conditional rules so new team members can understand what the value means in practice.

When promoting or assigning leaders to new locations, ensure they fully understand and visibly model all codified culture rules and reinforcement patterns; do not rely on the original culture champion to sustain culture passively.

Use explicit rule codification (the comprehensive approach) rather than the 'fast and dirty' approach (vague value descriptions); the extra work in rule definition enables consistent enforcement and reduces ambiguity during scaling.
